courseTitle: Research Methods in Applied Linguistics and ELT
overview:
Course E413, Research Methods in Applied Linguistics and English Language Teaching (ELT), equips undergraduate scholars with the foundational paradigms, empirical designs, and analytical competencies required to investigate language learning, teaching, and usage systematically. The course structures the research journey into six interconnected stages: conceptual foundations, problem formulation, research design, empirical sampling and instrumentation, data processing and analysis, and academic reporting.

Students explore the methodological continuum spanning quantitative experimental and survey paradigms, qualitative traditions (narrative inquiry, ethnography, case study, and grounded theory), digital discourse, corpus linguistics, psycholinguistic experimentation, and critical discourse analysis (CDA). Rigorous attention is given to the formulation of research questions, operationalization of variables, synthesis of literature, and identification of research gaps. Methodological procedures emphasize representative probability and purposive sampling, validated instrumentation (questionnaires, interviews, classroom observation schemes like COLT and TALOS), and multi-method triangulation to safeguard validity, reliability, and ethical integrity.

For data analysis, the course integrates qualitative coding hierarchies (verbatim transcription, open, axial, and thematic analysis) with quantitative descriptive statistics (central tendency, dispersion, standard deviation) and inferential hypothesis testing (t-tests, ANOVA, Chi-square, Pearson correlation). Finally, the curriculum guides students in preparing formal research proposals, dissertations, and academic papers adhering strictly to APA 7th edition standards, ethical safeguards, and plagiarism prevention protocols, preparing candidates for both their undergraduate dissertations and rigorous viva voce examinations.

topics.title: Research Concept, Nature, and Quality
topics.coreIdea: Research is a careful, systematic inquiry that collects and analyses empirical evidence to answer questions, solve problems, or advance knowledge. In applied linguistics, it transforms subjective classroom impressions into rigorous, verifiable findings governed by controlled, empirical, and critical inquiry.
topics.vivaAnswer: Research in applied linguistics is a systematic, evidence-based inquiry that investigates language learning, teaching, or use. It requires a clear question, justified methodology, empirical evidence, and critical interpretation rather than unsupported personal opinion.
topics.example: Investigating whether role-play improves EFL speaking fluency by measuring words per minute before and after a four-week intervention under controlled conditions.
topics.understandMore: The teacher's slides outline eight sequential research stages: formulating the problem, choosing the research design, constructing the instrument, selecting the sample, writing the proposal, collecting data, processing and displaying data, and writing the report. High-quality research exhibits six core characteristics: controlled (isolating variables), rigorous (methodological discipline), systematic (logical sequence), valid and verifiable (accurate and replicable), empirical (grounded in observable evidence), and critical (scrutinizing procedures and limitations).
topics.commonConfusion: A pedagogical activity or personal opinion is not research; research requires an explicit problem statement, systematic data collection, principled analysis, and peer-scrutinized evidence.

topics.title: Research Paradigms: Qualitative, Quantitative, and Mixed Methods
topics.coreIdea: Research paradigms determine the epistemological stance, data types, and logic used in inquiry. Quantitative research relies on deductive logic and numerical measurement to test hypotheses, qualitative research uses inductive logic and rich descriptive data to understand human meanings in context, and mixed methods purposefully integrates both.
topics.vivaAnswer: Quantitative research tests hypotheses using numerical measurements and statistical analysis, while qualitative research explores experiences and meanings in natural contexts using non-numerical data. Mixed methods integrates both to provide a more comprehensive explanation than either approach alone.
topics.example: Using a pre/post-test speaking score (quantitative) alongside learner diary entries and semi-structured interviews (qualitative) to evaluate the impact and learner experiences of task-based language teaching.
topics.understandMore: Quantitative approaches assume an objective, measurable reality and aim for generalizability, objectivity, and causal explanation. Qualitative approaches assume socially constructed, multiple realities, prioritizing depth, context, authenticity, and emic (insider) perspectives. Mixed-methods research is not merely adding open-ended questions to a survey; it requires deliberate integration of qualitative and quantitative strands during data collection, analysis, or interpretation.
topics.commonConfusion: Collecting both numbers and words does not constitute mixed methods unless the two forms of data are systematically integrated to answer complementary research questions.

topics.title: Research Classification Bases
topics.coreIdea: Research studies can be classified along multiple independent dimensions rather than mutually exclusive boxes. Key classification bases include application (pure vs applied), objective (descriptive, exploratory, explanatory, correlational), mode of inquiry (qualitative vs quantitative), manipulation (experimental vs observational), time (cross-sectional vs longitudinal), and setting (field, laboratory, documentary).
topics.vivaAnswer: Studies are classified across eight different dimensions: application, objective, mode of inquiry, researcher manipulation, logical inference, time frame, information source, and data-collection setting. These describe different features of the same study simultaneously.
topics.example: A study testing phonological pronunciation software in a university sound booth across one semester is simultaneously applied, explanatory, quantitative, experimental, longitudinal, primary, and laboratory-based.
topics.understandMore: Lecture 02 identifies eight distinct classification bases: (1) Application (pure/basic vs applied), (2) Objective (descriptive, exploratory, explanatory, correlational), (3) Mode of enquiry (qualitative, quantitative, mixed), (4) Manipulation (experimental, quasi-experimental, observational), (5) Inference (deductive vs inductive), (6) Time (cross-sectional snapshot vs longitudinal tracking), (7) Information source (primary vs secondary), and (8) Setting (field, laboratory, documentary, or combined).
topics.commonConfusion: Students often treat these classifications as competing categories; in reality, a single research study is categorized on every one of these eight dimensions.

topics.title: Problem Formulation, Significance, and the Four Ps
topics.coreIdea: A research problem is an intellectual uncertainty, practical difficulty, or gap in knowledge that gives a study focus, rationale, and scope. Sources of problems in ELT are encapsulated by the Four Ps: People (learners/teachers), Problems (learning barriers), Programmes (curricula/interventions), and Phenomena (language practices).
topics.vivaAnswer: A research problem identifies what is unsatisfactory, unresolved, or poorly understood in a specific context. It draws from the 'Four Ps'—People, Problems, Programmes, and Phenomena—and establishes why the inquiry is academically and practically significant.
topics.example: Examining why undergraduate Bengali speakers experience high oral anxiety (Problem) during English communicative tasks (Phenomenon) in a tertiary speaking programme (Programme) involving first-year students (People).
topics.understandMore: Formulating a research problem involves moving from a broad topic (e.g., EFL speaking) to a specific, manageable problem statement that details what is uncertain and why it matters. The significance of the study must justify seven dimensions: field relevance, practical classroom implications, theoretical contribution, societal needs, advancement of knowledge, future research directions, and benefits to stakeholders (teachers, learners, policymakers).
topics.commonConfusion: Confusing a broad topic (e.g., 'Grammar in ELT') with a research problem; a problem must pinpoint a specific tension, contradiction, or empirical unknown.

topics.title: Research Questions, Objectives, Hypotheses, and Variables
topics.coreIdea: Research questions specify what the study will investigate, objectives declare what the researcher aims to achieve using operational action verbs, and hypotheses offer testable predictions. In quantitative designs, variables represent characteristics that take on different values and must be operationalized.
topics.vivaAnswer: A research question asks what the study will answer, an objective outlines the concrete actions to achieve it, and a hypothesis predicts the expected relationship between variables. Operational definitions specify exactly how abstract constructs like 'fluency' or 'anxiety' will be measured.
topics.example: RQ: Does extensive reading increase EFL vocabulary size? Objective: To compare vocabulary gains between extensive and intensive reading groups. Hypothesis: Learners engaging in extensive reading will achieve significantly higher post-test vocabulary scores.
topics.understandMore: Variables are classified by role: Independent Variable (IV, presumed cause or intervention), Dependent Variable (DV, measured outcome), Extraneous/Confounding Variables (uncontrolled factors that threaten internal validity), Moderating Variables (factors that alter the strength or direction of the IV-DV relationship), and Mediating/Intervening Variables (factors that explain the psychological or linguistic mechanism connecting IV and DV). Operational definitions convert theoretical constructs into measurable indicators (e.g., measuring speaking fluency as words produced per minute).
topics.commonConfusion: Students confuse null hypotheses with research hypotheses. The null hypothesis (H0) predicts no significant difference or relationship, whereas the alternative hypothesis (H1) posits a significant effect.

topics.title: Literature Review and the Seven Research Gaps
topics.coreIdea: A literature review is a critical, synthesized evaluation of published scholarship that maps existing knowledge, identifies methodological approaches, and justifies the study by establishing an authentic research gap. The guide identifies seven distinct types of research gaps.
topics.vivaAnswer: A literature review synthesizes and critically evaluates previous studies to establish what is known, what is debated, and what remains missing. It justifies the study by demonstrating a specific research gap, such as an empirical, theoretical, or population gap.
topics.example: Synthesizing fifteen empirical studies on corrective feedback and showing that while oral feedback has been examined in secondary schools, virtually no evidence exists regarding tertiary writing feedback in Bangladeshi universities (a population and context gap).
topics.understandMore: The literature review requires five sequential stages: searching literature using precise keywords, evaluating and selecting credible sources, identifying recurring themes and gaps, planning an organizing structure (chronological, thematic, methodological, or theoretical), and writing the synthesis. The seven research gaps are: (1) Population/context gap (unstudied demographic or setting), (2) Conceptual gap (unclear or conflicting definitions), (3) Empirical gap (lack of observable data), (4) Evidence gap (contradictory findings across studies), (5) Theoretical gap (absence or failure of explanatory theory), (6) Methodology gap (limitation in previous methods, e.g., relying solely on self-reports), and (7) Practical gap (disconnect between research recommendations and real classroom practice).
topics.commonConfusion: A literature review is not an annotated bibliography or a mere list of article summaries ('A said X, B said Y'); it must synthesize patterns, critique methodological limitations, and justify the current study.

topics.title: Experimental and Quasi-Experimental Research Designs
topics.coreIdea: Experimental research deliberately manipulates an independent variable to observe its causal effect on a dependent variable while controlling extraneous factors. True experiments feature random assignment of participants to experimental and control conditions, whereas quasi-experiments evaluate interventions using intact, non-randomized groups.
topics.vivaAnswer: An experiment tests causality by manipulating an independent variable, holding confounding factors constant, and measuring changes in a dependent variable. True experiments use random assignment to conditions, whereas quasi-experiments work with intact classroom groups.
topics.example: A pretest-posttest control-group design where two existing Grade 9 classes are assigned to either a gamified vocabulary app (experimental) or traditional word lists (control), with vocabulary knowledge tested before and after six weeks.
topics.understandMore: Experimental notation uses R (random assignment), X (treatment), and O (observation/test). Key experimental designs include: (1) Pretest-posttest control-group design (R: O1 X O2; R: O3 - O4), (2) Posttest-only control-group design (R: X O1; R: - O2, avoiding pretest sensitization), (3) Factorial designs (evaluating two or more IVs simultaneously and detecting interaction effects, such as feedback type × proficiency level), (4) Repeated-measures designs (measuring the same participants under multiple conditions), and (5) Solomon four-group designs (combining pretested and unpretested groups to isolate testing effects).
topics.commonConfusion: Students frequently confuse random selection (how participants enter a sample from a population) with random assignment (how sampled participants are allocated to treatment or control groups).

topics.title: Survey Research in Applied Linguistics
topics.coreIdea: Survey research systematically collects demographic, behavioural, and attitudinal data from a sample to describe characteristics or examine relationships within a wider population. Surveys can be cross-sectional (a single snapshot in time) or longitudinal (tracking change over time via trend, cohort, or panel designs).
topics.vivaAnswer: Survey research gathers demographic, behavioural, or attitudinal data from a representative sample using questionnaires or structured interviews to describe patterns and associations across a population.
topics.example: Administering a Likert-scale questionnaire to 300 university learners across five faculties to investigate self-reported English learning anxiety and autonomous study habits.
topics.understandMore: Surveys capture three main data types: descriptive/demographic (who respondents are), behavioural (what respondents report doing, such as daily reading hours), and preference/opinion (attitudes, beliefs, satisfaction). Longitudinal survey designs include: (1) Trend studies (measuring the general population at different times using different samples), (2) Cohort studies (tracking a specific subpopulation identified by a shared milestone, e.g., the Class of 2024), and (3) Panel studies (measuring the exact same individuals repeatedly over successive time intervals). The seven survey stages are: planning, sampling design, instrument construction, data collection, data preparation/cleaning, analysis, and reporting.
topics.commonConfusion: A survey is a comprehensive research design and methodology, whereas a questionnaire is merely one data-collection instrument used within a survey.

topics.title: Case Study Research in Applied Linguistics
topics.coreIdea: A case study is an empirical inquiry that investigates a contemporary phenomenon in depth within its real-world context, especially when the boundaries between phenomenon and context are not clearly evident. In applied linguistics, a case is a bounded system—such as a single learner, a teacher, a classroom, or a language programme.
topics.vivaAnswer: A case study is an in-depth, multifaceted investigation of a single bounded system—such as a language learner, classroom, or institution—in its natural context, using multiple sources of empirical evidence.
topics.example: Conducting a semester-long intrinsic case study of an immigrant adult beginner learning English in an evening community class, using interviews, weekly journal entries, and classroom recordings to understand language identity development.
topics.understandMore: Key case study theorists include Robert Stake and Robert Yin. The guide outlines six case study typologies: (1) Intrinsic (understanding an unusual or unique case for its own inherent merit), (2) Instrumental (examining a specific case to illuminate a broader issue or refine theory), (3) Collective/Multiple (comparing several bounded cases to identify cross-case patterns), (4) Holistic (analyzing the case as one unified, global entity), (5) Embedded (analyzing distinct subunits within the overarching case), and (6) Longitudinal (following a bounded case across extended developmental time).
topics.commonConfusion: Case studies do not aim for statistical generalizability to a wider population; instead, they provide analytical or theoretical generalizability (transferability) and rich contextual insight.

topics.title: Ethnography and Classroom Observation
topics.coreIdea: Ethnography investigates the shared culture, social practices, and meanings of a language community or classroom through sustained participant observation and immersive fieldwork. Observation ranges across structured checklists, semi-structured protocols, and unstructured field notes, utilizing established observation schemes like COLT and TALOS.
topics.vivaAnswer: Ethnography studies the shared cultural and communicative practices of a group through immersive fieldwork, aiming for an emic or insider perspective. Classroom observation captures live interaction using structured observation schemes like COLT or TALOS alongside detailed field notes.
topics.example: Spending an academic year observing peer interactions in an English-medium primary school classroom, taking reflexive field notes on how code-switching negotiates social inclusion.
topics.understandMore: Ethnography emphasizes the dialectic between the emic (insider participant perspective) and etic (outsider analytical perspective). Observation varies along four distinct axes: (1) Planning/structure (structured checklist vs semi-structured vs unstructured), (2) Observer role (Raymond Gold's continuum: complete participant, participant-as-observer, observer-as-participant, complete observer), (3) Setting (naturalistic classroom vs controlled laboratory), and (4) Disclosure (overt vs covert). Standard ELT schemes include COLT (Communicative Orientation of Language Teaching, measuring communicative features of classrooms) and TALOS (Target Language Observation Scheme).
topics.commonConfusion: Observation provides direct evidence of actual classroom behaviour, but it cannot directly reveal internal cognitive states, feelings, or attitudes, which require interviews or introspective instruments.

topics.title: Action Research and Narrative Inquiry
topics.coreIdea: Action research is a reflective, practitioner-led cyclical inquiry designed to diagnose practical classroom problems and implement immediate pedagogical improvements. Narrative inquiry explores teachers' and learners' lived experiences and professional identities through personal stories, autobiographies, and reflective narratives.
topics.vivaAnswer: Action research is a cyclical, reflective inquiry conducted by classroom practitioners using the Plan-Act-Observe-Reflect cycle to solve local teaching challenges. Narrative inquiry investigates language learning and teaching through personal stories and lived experiences over time.
topics.example: An English teacher noticing low student participation during group reading, introducing jigsaw reading tasks, observing peer interactions, and reflecting on how to refine the task in the next cycle.
topics.understandMore: Action research originated with Kurt Lewin and was developed in education by Stephen Kemmis and Anne Burns in ELT. It follows a four-stage spiral: (1) Plan an intervention, (2) Act by implementing it, (3) Observe the process and effects, and (4) Reflect on outcomes to begin the next cycle. Narrative inquiry (championed by Clandinin & Connelly, and Gary Barkhuizen in ELT) conceptualizes human experience as narrative, using narrative frames, language learning histories, and life-history interviews to examine learner identity, agency, and emotion in language acquisition.
topics.commonConfusion: Action research is not intended for generalizable theoretical claims across all universities; its primary aim is localized pedagogical action and professional development in a specific classroom.
topics.sourceRef: E413 Guide pp. 6, 26 + Supplementary (Standard AL/ELT Research Methodology)

topics.title: Grounded Theory and Qualitative Interpretive Approaches
topics.coreIdea: Grounded Theory Method (GTM) is an inductive qualitative methodology that generates theoretical models directly grounded in empirical data rather than testing existing theories. Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis (IPA) investigates how participants make psychological sense of major lived experiences.
topics.vivaAnswer: Grounded theory develops an inductive theoretical model grounded systematically in collected empirical data, using constant comparison and theoretical sampling until theoretical saturation is achieved.
topics.example: Interviewing thirty non-native English novice teachers across two years to construct an emergent grounded theory explaining how teachers navigate professional identity crisis in English-medium universities.
topics.understandMore: Formulated by Barney Glaser and Anselm Strauss (1967) and later adapted into constructivist grounded theory by Kathy Charmaz (2006), GTM relies on core iterative techniques: (1) Theoretical sampling (selecting new participants based on concepts emerging from ongoing analysis), (2) Constant comparative method (comparing new data constantly against previously coded data and emerging categories), and (3) Theoretical saturation (the point where no new conceptual properties or insights emerge from additional data). In contrast, Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis (Jonathan Smith) has an idiographic focus, deeply exploring how individual participants perceive and interpret significant personal transitions.
topics.commonConfusion: Simply using thematic coding does not make a study Grounded Theory; GTM explicitly requires theoretical sampling, constant comparison, and the formulation of an integrated explanatory model.
topics.sourceRef: E413 Guide pp. 26-27 + Supplementary (Standard AL/ELT Research Methodology)

topics.title: Discourse Analysis (DA) and Critical Discourse Analysis (CDA)
topics.coreIdea: Discourse Analysis examines how spoken and written language operates in social interaction beyond the sentence level. Critical Discourse Analysis (CDA) explicitly investigates how language constructs, maintains, and challenges ideological dominance, institutional power asymmetries, and social inequalities.
topics.vivaAnswer: Discourse analysis investigates language in use above the sentence level to understand communicative functions. Critical Discourse Analysis (CDA) goes further by examining how discourse produces, reproduces, and legitimizes power relations, ideology, and social inequality.
topics.example: Analyzing English textbook dialogues to reveal how gender roles and socioeconomic status are stereotyped, showing how elite standard English is positioned as superior to regional vernaculars.
topics.understandMore: Prominent CDA theorists include Norman Fairclough, Teun van Dijk, and Ruth Wodak. Fairclough's influential three-dimensional model analyzes: (1) Text (formal linguistic features, vocabulary, grammar, metaphor), (2) Discursive Practice (processes of text production, distribution, and consumption), and (3) Social Practice (hegemonic structures, ideological power relations, and institutional context). Teun van Dijk focuses on socio-cognitive dimensions (mental models and shared social representations of elite dominance), while Ruth Wodak advances the discourse-historical approach, tracing how historical contexts shape discriminatory discourses. CDA connects directly to Michel Foucault's post-structuralist concepts of discourse and power/knowledge.
topics.commonConfusion: Ordinary discourse analysis describes communicative cohesion, turn-taking, or speech acts neutrally; CDA is openly emancipatory, political, and committed to exposing ideological injustice.
topics.sourceRef: E413 Guide p. 26 + Supplementary (Standard AL/ELT Research Methodology)

topics.title: Corpus Linguistics and Digital Discourse Research
topics.coreIdea: Corpus research utilizes large, principled, electronically stored collections of natural texts to uncover empirical patterns of word frequency, collocation, and grammatical usage. Digital discourse research investigates language in computer-mediated communication, online social platforms, and multimodal digital environments.
topics.vivaAnswer: Corpus research analyzes large electronic databases of real spoken or written texts using computational tools to investigate authentic language frequencies and collocations. Digital discourse research explores communicative practices in online, computer-mediated environments.
topics.example: Searching a one-million-word learner corpus of university essays (such as ICLE) using concordancing software to examine common preposition errors and formulaic lexical collocations.
topics.understandMore: Corpus linguistics (pioneered by John Sinclair and Douglas Biber) uses specialized metrics: concordances (keyword in context / KWIC displays), collocations (words co-occurring with statistical significance, measured by MI score or t-score), clusters/n-grams, and keywords. Learner corpora compare non-native language against native corpora (e.g., BNC or COCA) to inform pedagogical materials and dictionaries. Digital discourse research (Rodney Jones, David Crystal) analyzes computer-mediated communication (CMC), hypertext, multimodal memes, emojis, and asynchronous forums, addressing methodological issues such as screen-scraping ethics, dynamic text boundaries, and digital identities.
topics.commonConfusion: A corpus is not a single textbook or small reading list; it must be a principled, balanced, and machine-searchable sample of authentic language designed according to strict design criteria.

topics.title: Psycholinguistic Methods and Critical/Interdisciplinary Research
topics.coreIdea: Psycholinguistic methodology uses controlled behavioral and neuroimaging experiments to measure real-time language processing, comprehension, and production. Interdisciplinary and critical research integrates cognitive, sociological, and pedagogical lenses to explore complex linguistic realities.
topics.vivaAnswer: Psycholinguistic methods measure real-time cognitive language processing using experimental techniques like reaction-time recording, eye-tracking, and ERPs. Critical and interdisciplinary research blends linguistics with sociology, psychology, and education to address complex language issues.
topics.example: Using a self-paced reading task or eye-tracking to record reading times at a garden-path syntactic boundary in second language learners, identifying where parsing breakdown occurs.
topics.understandMore: Psycholinguistic experimental paradigms include: (1) Reaction time (RT) measurements, (2) Eye-tracking (measuring fixations, saccades, and regressions), (3) Self-paced reading/listening, (4) Priming experiments (semantic, lexical, or syntactic priming), (5) Grammaticality judgment tasks (GJTs), and (6) Neuroimaging techniques such as Event-Related Potentials (ERPs), where the N400 wave marks semantic anomalies and the P600 marks syntactic violations. Critical applied linguistics (Alastair Pennycook) integrates linguistic research with socio-political critique, interrogating linguistic imperialism (Robert Phillipson) and native-speakerism (Adrian Holliday).
topics.commonConfusion: Offline tasks (like pen-and-paper fill-in-the-blank tests) measure explicit, metalinguistic knowledge, whereas online psycholinguistic measures (like eye-tracking or ERPs) tap implicit, millisecond-by-millisecond cognitive processing.

topics.title: Population, Sampling Techniques, and Research Ethics
topics.coreIdea: Sampling selects a representative subgroup from a target population to enable empirical investigation and valid inference. Sampling divides into probability methods (simple random, stratified, cluster, systematic) and non-probability methods (purposive, convenience, snowball, quota), governed by strict ethical standards.
topics.vivaAnswer: Sampling selects participants from a target population. Probability sampling gives every member a known, non-zero chance of selection enabling statistical generalization, whereas non-probability sampling selects participants purposefully or conveniently for qualitative depth.
topics.example: Using stratified random sampling to select 200 EFL learners across four university faculties proportionate to faculty enrollment, ensuring balanced representation of humanities, science, and business students.
topics.understandMore: Target population is the complete group of interest; sampling frame is the actual operational list from which cases are drawn; sample is the selected subgroup. Probability sampling methods include: Simple Random (equal lottery chance), Stratified Random (dividing population into homogeneous strata and sampling proportionally), Cluster Sampling (randomly selecting intact clusters like whole schools), and Systematic Sampling (selecting every kth individual from a list). Non-probability methods include: Purposive/Judgmental (selecting information-rich cases), Convenience (accessible subjects), Snowball (participants recruit further participants, ideal for hidden populations), and Quota sampling. Research ethics requires informed consent, voluntary participation, confidentiality/anonymity, right to withdraw, and prevention of harm.
topics.commonConfusion: Confusing anonymity with confidentiality. Anonymity means the researcher never knows the participant's identity; confidentiality means the researcher knows the identity but protects it from disclosure.

topics.title: Questionnaires and Questionnaire Response Formats
topics.coreIdea: A questionnaire is a structured self-report instrument consisting of written items designed to capture respondents' demographic data, behaviours, or attitudes. Response formats include closed items (Likert scales, semantic differential, rating scales, multiple-choice) and open-ended questions, requiring careful piloting to prevent design flaws.
topics.vivaAnswer: A questionnaire gathers self-reported data using closed or open-ended items. Effective questionnaire design requires clear, unbiased wording, validated response formats like Likert scales, and rigorous pilot testing to ensure reliability.
topics.example: A 5-point Likert questionnaire measuring student attitudes toward peer feedback, ranging from 1 (Strongly Disagree) to 5 (Strongly Agree).
topics.understandMore: Questionnaires can be closed (fixed response), open-ended (free text), or mixed. Key response formats: (1) Likert-type agreement scales (typically 5 or 6 points), (2) Semantic differential (rating between bipolar opposite adjectives, e.g., 'boring' 1-5 'engaging'), (3) Numerical rating scales, (4) Dichotomous items (Yes/No), (5) Multiple choice, and (6) Rank order. Major item-writing flaws to avoid include double-barrelled items (asking two questions in one item), leading questions (cueing the desired response), vague time references ('often' vs 'past week'), confusing double negatives, and social desirability bias. Piloting is essential to detect ambiguities before full deployment.
topics.commonConfusion: A self-reported response on a questionnaire shows only what participants believe or claim about their learning; it cannot measure actual language acquisition or objective proficiency gains.

topics.title: Interviews, Focus Group Discussions, and Triangulation
topics.coreIdea: Interviews and focus groups are interactive qualitative data-collection methods that elicit participants' lived experiences, meanings, and perspectives. Triangulation combines multiple data sources, investigators, theories, or methods to enhance credibility and cross-validate findings.
topics.vivaAnswer: Interviews gather rich individual accounts through structured, semi-structured, or unstructured formats, while Focus Group Discussions capitalize on group interaction. Triangulation integrates multiple data sources or methods to cross-validate findings and eliminate blind spots.
topics.example: Combining classroom observation field notes, student survey responses, and teacher semi-structured interviews (methodological triangulation) to investigate classroom silence.
topics.understandMore: Interviews vary by structure: Structured (fixed script and questions), Semi-structured (guiding interview guide with flexible probing), Unstructured (open conversational dialogue), and In-depth (intensive biographical exploration). Focus Group Discussions (FGDs, typically 6-10 participants) use a moderator to stimulate debate and explore shared norms, though moderators must actively prevent dominant speakers from suppressing quiet voices. Norman Denzin's four types of triangulation are: (1) Data triangulation (collecting data across different times, spaces, and people), (2) Investigator triangulation (employing multiple researchers in data collection and coding), (3) Theory triangulation (interpreting data through multiple theoretical perspectives), and (4) Methodological triangulation (between-method or within-method approaches).
topics.commonConfusion: Triangulation is not conducted solely to make data match; divergent or contradictory findings between interviews and observations are valuable findings that illuminate complex social dynamics.

topics.title: Qualitative Data Analysis: Transcription, Coding, and Themes
topics.coreIdea: Qualitative data analysis transforms unstructured verbal or visual text into meaningful patterns and theoretical explanations. It progresses through transcription, open and axial coding, category construction, and thematic interpretation.
topics.vivaAnswer: Qualitative data analysis is an interpretive process that moves from raw transcripts to codes, categories, and overarching themes. In thematic analysis, researchers systematically identify, analyze, and report patterned meanings across a qualitative dataset.
topics.example: Coding thirty interview transcripts to group codes like 'fear of peer laughter' and 'fear of teacher correction' under the category 'evaluative anxiety', which forms the theme 'Social Risk in Classroom Speaking'.
topics.understandMore: Transcription types include: Verbatim (capturing exact words, fillers, pauses, and laughter), Intelligent Verbatim (removing non-essential hesitations for readability without altering meaning), and Edited Transcription (summarized text). The coding pipeline moves from raw data to: (1) Open coding (generating initial conceptual labels for meaningful segments), (2) Axial coding (clustering related codes into conceptual categories and linking subcategories), (3) Selective coding (identifying the central core category), (4) Themes (broad recurring patterns answering the RQs), and (5) Thematic interpretation. Braun and Clarke's (2006) 6 phases of Thematic Analysis are: familiarization, generating initial codes, searching for themes, reviewing themes, defining/naming themes, and producing the report.
topics.commonConfusion: Thematic analysis does not simply summarize transcript quotes or count keyword frequencies; it interprets underlying socio-cultural meanings, tensions, and latent assumptions.

topics.title: Quantitative Data Analysis: Descriptive Statistics
topics.coreIdea: Descriptive statistics organize, summarize, and display numerical data to describe the characteristics of a sample. Key techniques include frequency distributions, measures of central tendency (mean, median, mode), and measures of dispersion (range, variance, standard deviation).
topics.vivaAnswer: Descriptive statistics summarize and describe sample data through measures of central tendency—mean, median, and mode—and measures of dispersion, primarily standard deviation, showing how scores spread around the average.
topics.example: Reporting that an EFL grammar class achieved a mean pre-test score of 52.4 with a standard deviation of 8.2, showing that most scores clustered between 44.2 and 60.6.
topics.understandMore: Central tendency: (1) Mean (arithmetic average, sensitive to extreme outliers), (2) Median (middle score in an ordered distribution, unaffected by extreme outliers and ideal for skewed data), and (3) Mode (most frequent score, useful for nominal or categorical data). Dispersion: Range (difference between maximum and minimum), Variance (average of squared deviations from the mean), and Standard Deviation (square root of variance, returning the dispersion metric to the original scale of measurement: s = sqrt[sum(x - mean)^2 / (n - 1)]). A larger standard deviation indicates greater variability among learners.
topics.commonConfusion: A high standard deviation simply indicates wider score dispersion; it does not indicate whether a teaching method was effective or whether group differences are statistically significant.

topics.title: Quantitative Data Analysis: Inferential Statistics
topics.coreIdea: Inferential statistics use probability theory and sample evidence to draw conclusions about population parameters and test formal research hypotheses. Common statistical tests in ELT include t-tests, ANOVA, Chi-square tests, Pearson's correlation, z-tests, and factor analysis.
topics.vivaAnswer: Inferential statistics allow researchers to test hypotheses and draw conclusions about a wider population from sample data. Standard tests include t-tests for two group means, ANOVA for three or more groups, Chi-square for categorical data, and Pearson's r for correlations.
topics.example: Conducting an independent-samples t-test to determine if the mean vocabulary gain of a mobile-assisted learning group is significantly higher than that of a conventional textbook group (p < .05).
topics.understandMore: Key inferential concepts and tests include: (1) p-value and significance level (typically alpha = .05, meaning less than 5% probability that the observed result occurred by chance under the null hypothesis), (2) Type I error (rejecting a true null hypothesis, false positive) vs Type II error (failing to reject a false null hypothesis, false negative), (3) Independent-samples t-test (comparing means of two unrelated groups), (4) Paired-samples t-test (comparing pre- and post-test means from the same participants), (5) One-way ANOVA (comparing means across three or more groups, avoiding family-wise error rate), (6) Chi-square (chi^2) test of independence (testing associations between two categorical variables, e.g., gender vs preferred learning style), (7) Pearson's correlation coefficient r (measuring linear relationship between continuous variables from -1.0 to +1.0; correlation does not imply causation), (8) z-test (comparing sample mean to population mean when population variance is known and n >= 30), and (9) Factor analysis (a data-reduction technique identifying underlying latent dimensions across observed variables).
topics.commonConfusion: A statistically significant finding (p < .05) does not automatically mean the effect is practically meaningful or large; researchers should always examine effect size (e.g., Cohen's d).
topics.sourceRef: E413 Guide p. 29 + Supplementary (Standard AL/ELT Research Methodology)

topics.title: Presentation of Findings, Discussion, and Conclusion
topics.coreIdea: Research reporting separates the objective presentation of findings from their critical interpretation in the discussion. The conclusion synthesizes primary inferences, delineates actionable pedagogical recommendations, and transparently acknowledges research limitations.
topics.vivaAnswer: The Findings (Results) section objectively presents what the empirical evidence shows without editorial commentary. The Discussion interprets what those findings mean, connecting them back to research questions, theoretical frameworks, and previous literature.
topics.example: Presenting test score tables and statistical t-values in Chapter 4 (Results), then analyzing why communicative role-play reduced anxiety in Chapter 5 (Discussion) by referencing Krashen's Affective Filter Hypothesis and earlier studies.
topics.understandMore: The Results section organizes data logically around research questions, presenting quantitative statistical summaries (means, standard deviations, test statistics, degrees of freedom, p-values) alongside qualitative themes with illustrative interview extracts. The Discussion chapter performs five critical functions: answering the research questions directly, comparing findings against the literature review, interpreting theoretical and pedagogical implications, explaining contradictory or unexpected results, and evaluating limitations. The Conclusion chapter summarizes key insights, draws overarching inferences, provides concrete pedagogical recommendations, and proposes avenues for future research.
topics.commonConfusion: Do not repeat raw descriptive data or statistical calculations in the Discussion; the Discussion must explain mechanisms, justify conclusions, and engage with scholarly debates.

topics.title: Academic Documentation, Citations, and Plagiarism Prevention
topics.coreIdea: Academic documentation credits intellectual sources, provides an audit trail for claims, and prevents plagiarism. In-text citations can be parenthetical or narrative, and scholarly writing requires principled distinctions between direct quotations, paraphrases, and summaries.
topics.vivaAnswer: Citation acknowledges the intellectual property of other scholars, supports empirical claims, and upholds academic integrity. Plagiarism—presenting another's words, data, or ideas as one's own—is avoided through accurate quoting, rigorous paraphrasing, and consistent referencing.
topics.example: Writing a narrative citation: 'Ellis (2015) argues that task-based language teaching fosters communicative fluency,' versus a parenthetical citation: '(Ellis, 2015)'.
topics.understandMore: In-text citations link borrowed concepts to the terminal reference list. A direct quotation reproduces exact wording (under 40 words enclosed in quotation marks; 40 or more words set as an indented block quote) and requires author, publication year, and specific page/locator (e.g., Rahman, 2024, p. 12). A paraphrase rewrites an idea completely in the author's own original syntax and vocabulary, requiring author and year. A summary condenses the broader thesis of an entire work. Plagiarism encompasses direct copy-pasting, mosaic plagiarism/patchwriting (changing isolated words while copying sentence architecture), self-plagiarism, and improper paraphrasing. In universities (e.g., Jahangirnagar University), a similarity index threshold (typically maximum 25%) is enforced via Turnitin.
topics.commonConfusion: Changing a few synonyms in a copied paragraph while leaving the grammatical structure intact is still plagiarism (patchwriting); genuine paraphrasing requires original language and complete sentence reconstruction.

topics.title: APA Style (7th Edition) Referencing Rules
topics.coreIdea: The American Psychological Association (APA 7th edition) style governs formatting and documentation in applied linguistics and ELT. Key conventions include author-date citations, sentence case for book and article titles, title case and italics for journal titles, and standardized reference entries with DOIs.
topics.vivaAnswer: APA 7th edition uses author-date citations in-text and an alphabetical reference list at the end. For three or more authors, 'et al.' is used from the very first citation, and reference entries omit publisher locations while including active DOI URLs.
topics.example: Referencing an article: Dörnyei, Z. (2019). Towards a better understanding of L2 motivation. Language Teaching, 52(1), 19-30. https://doi.org/10.1017/S026144481800033X
topics.understandMore: Key APA 7 reference formats: (1) Whole Book: Author, A. A. (Year). Title of book: Subtitle (2nd ed.). Publisher. (Publisher city/location is omitted in APA 7). (2) Edited Book Chapter: Author, A. A. (Year). Title of chapter. In B. B. Editor & C. C. Editor (Eds.), Title of book (pp. 10-25). Publisher. (3) Journal Article: Author, A. A., & Author, B. B. (Year). Title of article. Title of Journal, 12(3), 45-60. https://doi.org/xxxx. (Article title in sentence case; journal title and volume number in italics; issue number in parentheses non-italicized). (4) Webpage: Author or Organization. (Year, Month Day). Title of page. Site Name. URL. In-text rules: For 1 author: (Rahman, 2024); for 2 authors: (Rahman & Sen, 2024) parenthetically and 'Rahman and Sen (2024)' narratively; for 3 or more authors: (Rahman et al., 2024) on all citations.
topics.commonConfusion: In APA 7, DO NOT use 'et al.' in the final reference list unless there are more than 20 authors. In the references, list up to 20 authors by surname and initials before using an ellipsis.

topics.title: Research Proposal, Dissertation/Thesis, and Academic Article Writing
topics.coreIdea: Academic writing in ELT spans research proposals (prospective plans demonstrating feasibility and justification), dissertations/theses (comprehensive retrospective reports across six standard chapters), and published research articles structured in IMRAD format.
topics.vivaAnswer: A research proposal outlines a planned study, explaining what will be studied, why it matters, and how it will be conducted. A dissertation reports the completed empirical study across six chapters: Introduction, Literature Review, Methodology, Results, Discussion, and Conclusion.
topics.example: Structuring an ELT Master's dissertation into six chapters: 1. Introduction, 2. Literature Review, 3. Methodology, 4. Results, 5. Discussion, and 6. Conclusion, accompanied by an abstract of 150-350 words.
topics.understandMore: A research proposal is written in future tense and includes: Title, Introduction & Problem Statement, Research Questions/Hypotheses, Significance, Literature Review, Theoretical/Conceptual Framework, Methodology (design, sampling, instruments, data analysis, ethics), Timeline, and Budget. A dissertation or thesis reports the actual completed study and follows a six-chapter model: Chapter 1: Introduction; Chapter 2: Literature Review; Chapter 3: Methodology; Chapter 4: Findings/Results; Chapter 5: Discussion; Chapter 6: Conclusion and Recommendations; followed by References and Appendices. Journal articles follow the standard IMRAD format (Introduction, Method, Results, And Discussion) along with an abstract and keywords, undergoing peer review prior to publication.
topics.commonConfusion: A proposal abstract describes planned objectives and proposed methods; it must never invent or report fictitious findings. A thesis abstract summarizes the completed study and actual findings.

questions.question: What is research in applied linguistics, and what distinguishes it from personal opinion?
questions.directAnswer: Research is a systematic, empirical inquiry collecting and analyzing evidence to answer a clear question, distinguished from opinion by rigorous, verifiable procedures.
questions.vivaAnswer: In applied linguistics, research is a careful, systematic investigation into language learning, teaching, or use. It transforms subjective opinions into verified knowledge by formulating clear questions, collecting observable evidence through justified methods, and critically interpreting the findings.
keyPoints: Systematic and controlled inquiry
Empirical evidence collection and analysis
Verifiable and peer-scrutinized methodology
questions.explanation: According to the course foundations, research moves from a question to an answer through evidence. Unlike mere personal impressions or teaching anecdotes, academic research requires an explicit problem statement, principled data-collection techniques, systematic data processing, and transparent reporting.

questions.question: What are the six essential characteristics or qualities of high-quality research identified in the course?
questions.directAnswer: The six essential qualities are: controlled, rigorous, systematic, valid and verifiable, empirical, and critical.
questions.vivaAnswer: High-quality research must be controlled to isolate variables, rigorous in following appropriate procedures, and systematic in its logical progression. Furthermore, it must be empirical, valid and verifiable, and critical in scrutinizing its own methods and limitations.
keyPoints: Controlled: minimizing extraneous interference
Rigorous and systematic: disciplined and logical stages
Empirical, verifiable, and critically evaluated
questions.explanation: These six qualities ensure that findings are credible. 'Controlled' means the researcher attempts to isolate the relationship between variables. 'Rigorous' demands relevant procedures. 'Systematic' follows an ordered sequence. 'Valid and verifiable' means observations can be checked and replicated. 'Empirical' requires real-world data. 'Critical' means procedures and conclusions are open to rigorous critique.

questions.question: How does pure or basic research differ from applied research in English Language Teaching?
questions.directAnswer: Pure research develops theories and fundamental knowledge, whereas applied research solves practical, immediate problems in language learning and teaching.
questions.vivaAnswer: Pure or basic research aims to formulate, test, or refine linguistic theories and understand fundamental language processes without immediate practical utility. In contrast, applied research in ELT addresses concrete real-world problems, such as evaluating instructional methods or designing language assessment tools.
keyPoints: Pure research: theory generation and fundamental knowledge
Applied research: practical problem-solving in educational contexts
Applied linguistics primarily emphasizes applied, decision-oriented inquiry
questions.explanation: Lecture 02 explains that classification by application distinguishes pure from applied inquiry. For example, studying the neural architecture of bilingual syntax is basic psycholinguistic research, whereas testing whether task-based pair work improves oral fluency in secondary classrooms is applied ELT research.

questions.question: What are the eight sequential steps in the research process outlined in the course?
questions.directAnswer: The eight steps are: formulate the problem, choose research design, construct instrument, select sample, write proposal, collect data, process and display data, and write report.
questions.vivaAnswer: The research journey moves through eight interconnected steps: first, formulating the research problem; second, choosing the design; third, constructing instruments; fourth, selecting the sample; fifth, writing the proposal; sixth, collecting data; seventh, processing and displaying findings; and eighth, writing the final report.
keyPoints: Sequential yet iterative research pipeline
Begins with problem definition and design choices
Culminates in data processing and formal thesis reporting
questions.explanation: While presented sequentially in Lecture 03, the teacher notes that this is an iterative process rather than a rigid one-way road. For instance, literature review continuously refines the problem and methodology, and in qualitative designs, data analysis often begins concurrently with data collection.

questions.question: How do quantitative and qualitative research paradigms differ in applied linguistics regarding data and logic?
questions.directAnswer: Quantitative research uses deductive logic and numerical data to test hypotheses, while qualitative research uses inductive logic and non-numerical data to explore subjective meanings.
questions.vivaAnswer: Quantitative research adopts a positivist stance, relying on deductive logic, standardized instruments, and statistical testing to uncover generalizable relationships. In contrast, qualitative research adopts an interpretivist stance, using inductive logic, rich verbal or visual data, and naturalistic inquiry to understand lived human experiences.
keyPoints: Quantitative: deductive, numerical, hypothesis-testing, objective measurement
Qualitative: inductive, non-numerical, exploratory, contextual understanding
Differences reflect underlying epistemology and research questions
questions.explanation: Quantitative studies operationalize variables into numerical scales (e.g., test scores, Likert ratings) and test pre-specified hypotheses. Qualitative studies collect open-ended data (e.g., interviews, field observations) to identify emergent patterns, perspectives, and social dynamics within real classrooms.

questions.question: What is mixed-methods research, and why is it particularly valuable in ELT inquiry?
questions.directAnswer: Mixed-methods research systematically integrates quantitative and qualitative data in a single study to achieve comprehensive understanding.
questions.vivaAnswer: Mixed-methods research deliberately combines quantitative and qualitative data collection and analytical procedures within a single study. In ELT, it is particularly valuable because quantitative data reveals broad trends or learning outcomes, while qualitative data uncovers the classroom experiences, teacher beliefs, and learner struggles behind those numbers.
keyPoints: Deliberate integration of numerical and textual strands
Provides both breadth (generalizability) and depth (contextual insight)
Overcomes the inherent weaknesses of single-method designs
questions.explanation: In an ELT context, examining speaking anxiety through a survey alone provides numerical scores but misses the personal narrative. Adding qualitative interviews explains why students feel anxious. The guide emphasizes that collecting both data types is only truly mixed-methods if they are explicitly integrated during analysis and interpretation.

questions.question: What is the difference between deductive reasoning and inductive reasoning in linguistic research?
questions.directAnswer: Deductive reasoning moves from general theory to specific hypothesis testing (top-down), whereas inductive reasoning moves from specific observations to broader generalizations and theory (bottom-up).
questions.vivaAnswer: Deductive reasoning is top-down logic where researchers start from an established theory, formulate testable hypotheses, and gather data to confirm or refute them. Inductive reasoning is bottom-up logic where researchers begin with open observations and build categories, patterns, and grounded theories directly from data.
keyPoints: Deductive: Theory -> Hypothesis -> Observation -> Confirmation (Top-down)
Inductive: Observation -> Pattern -> Tentative Hypothesis -> Theory (Bottom-up)
Quantitative aligns with deduction; qualitative aligns with induction
questions.explanation: An experimental ELT study testing Krashen's Input Hypothesis is deductive because it tests a pre-existing theory. An ethnography that observes communicative practices in a rural school to formulate a model of multilingual classroom participation is inductive.

questions.question: When should an applied linguist choose a qualitative research design rather than a quantitative one?
questions.directAnswer: When the research question seeks to explore personal experiences, social interactions, or complex cultural meanings that cannot be captured by numbers.
questions.vivaAnswer: A qualitative design should be chosen when the research problem is exploratory, little is known about the phenomenon, or the goal is to understand how participants interpret their lived experiences in context. It is ideal for investigating complex socio-cultural phenomena like language learner identity, teacher agency, and classroom power dynamics.
keyPoints: Exploration of poorly understood or novel phenomena
Investigation of subjective meanings, lived experiences, and identities
Need for rich contextual description rather than statistical generalization
questions.explanation: If a researcher wants to know 'What percentage of students suffer from speaking anxiety?', a quantitative survey is required. But if the question is 'How do immigrant adolescents negotiate their social identities in an English-medium classroom?', a qualitative design (such as narrative inquiry or ethnography) is essential.

questions.question: What eight distinct bases of research classification are identified in Lecture 02 of the course?
questions.directAnswer: The eight bases are: application, objective, mode of enquiry, manipulation, inference, time, information source, and data-collection setting.
questions.vivaAnswer: Lecture 02 classifies research across eight independent dimensions: application, research objective, mode of inquiry, manipulation of variables, logical inference, time perspective, information source, and data-collection setting.
keyPoints: Application (pure vs applied)
Objective, mode of enquiry, manipulation, inference
Time frame, information source, and physical setting
questions.explanation: These eight bases allow any empirical study to be classified comprehensively. For example, a single study can be described by its purpose (applied), its objective (explanatory), its data mode (quantitative), its intervention (experimental), its logic (deductive), its timeline (longitudinal), its source (primary), and its environment (laboratory).

questions.question: What is the critical distinction between cross-sectional and longitudinal research designs in applied linguistics?
questions.directAnswer: Cross-sectional research collects data from participants at a single point in time, whereas longitudinal research tracks participants across multiple time points to examine change.
questions.vivaAnswer: A cross-sectional study provides a snapshot of a population or compares different groups at one specific point in time. In contrast, a longitudinal study tracks the same or comparable participants over an extended period to investigate linguistic development, attrition, or pedagogical change over time.
keyPoints: Cross-sectional: single time point snapshot; fast and cost-effective
Longitudinal: diachronic tracking over multiple intervals; tracks actual growth
Cross-sectional shows associations; longitudinal provides evidence of development
questions.explanation: Comparing the vocabulary size of Year 1 and Year 4 university students in the same month is cross-sectional. Following a cohort of Year 1 students and re-testing their vocabulary every year until graduation is longitudinal. Cross-sectional data cannot directly prove individual developmental trajectory because cohort differences may confound the results.

questions.question: How do documentary, field, and laboratory research settings differ in language studies?
questions.directAnswer: Documentary studies examine existing texts, field research investigates language in its natural habitat, and laboratory research gathers data in artificially controlled environments.
questions.vivaAnswer: Documentary research analyzes existing textual records, such as curriculum policies or historical corpora. Field research collects data in natural real-world environments like ordinary classrooms, while laboratory research uses specially controlled environments, such as soundproof phonetics booths or eye-tracking labs, to isolate variables.
keyPoints: Documentary: textual archives, syllabi, textbooks, historical documents
Field: naturalistic settings, ordinary schools, authentic communities
Laboratory: artificial, strictly controlled physical environments
questions.explanation: Field research has high ecological validity because it observes authentic interactions, but has low experimental control. Laboratory research maximizes internal validity through strict environmental controls (e.g., sound isolation in phonetics), but may lack ecological authenticity.

questions.question: Why is combining data-collection settings (such as documentary and field) not automatically identical to mixed-methods research?
questions.directAnswer: Combining settings only varies the physical location of data collection, whereas mixed-methods research requires integrating both quantitative and qualitative paradigms.
questions.vivaAnswer: Combining settings refers to collecting data across multiple physical environments, such as analyzing curriculum documents and observing classrooms. However, a study is only 'mixed-methods' if it integrates both quantitative (numerical) and qualitative (textual) data and analysis; combining two qualitative field and documentary sources remains purely qualitative.
keyPoints: Setting refers to location (documentary, field, laboratory)
Mixed methods refers to integration of quantitative and qualitative paradigms
A multi-site study can be mono-methodological
questions.explanation: As noted on Page 6 of the guide, Lecture 02 loosely refers to combined settings as mixed settings. However, methodologically, analyzing historical policy documents (documentary) and interviewing teachers (field) is a multi-setting qualitative study, not a mixed-methods study, because both sources yield non-numerical, qualitative data.

questions.question: What is a research problem in applied linguistics, and how does it differ from a broad topic?
questions.directAnswer: A research problem is a specific uncertainty, difficulty, or gap in knowledge, whereas a topic is merely a general subject area.
questions.vivaAnswer: A research problem is an explicit, focused uncertainty, practical issue, or intellectual gap that requires empirical investigation. While a topic merely names a broad subject area like 'EFL speaking', a problem statement defines what is unsatisfactory or unresolved in a specific context and why it warrants investigation.
keyPoints: Topic: broad thematic domain (e.g., vocabulary acquisition)
Problem: specific difficulty, contradiction, or empirical unknown
Provides purpose, scope, and direction for research questions
questions.explanation: 'Second language writing' is a topic. A research problem states: 'Undergraduate students in English departments consistently demonstrate poor cohesive linking in argumentative essays despite explicit grammar instruction, and current pedagogical interventions fail to address discourse-level coherence.'

questions.question: What are the 'Four Ps' that serve as the primary sources of research problems in ELT?
questions.directAnswer: The Four Ps are: People, Problems, Programmes, and Phenomena.
questions.vivaAnswer: The Four Ps identify the sources of research problems: People (the participants or learners studied), Problems (the difficulties or issues they face), Programmes (the curricula, courses, or interventions evaluated), and Phenomena (the linguistic patterns or communicative practices observed).
keyPoints: People: the study population (learners, teachers)
Problems: learning difficulties, educational deficits
Programmes: instructional courses, teaching interventions
Phenomena: language practices, code-switching, anxiety
questions.explanation: Lecture 03 explains that 'People' provide the study population, while the other three Ps provide the subject matter. Most empirical studies combine two or more Ps; for instance, investigating first-year students' (People) evaluation of a remedial writing course (Programme) addresses both people and programme.

questions.question: What seven distinct aspects establish the significance or rationale of an applied linguistics study?
questions.directAnswer: The seven aspects are: relevance, practical implications, theoretical contribution, societal needs, advancement of knowledge, future research, and stakeholder relevance.
questions.vivaAnswer: The significance of a study explains why the problem matters across seven areas: its relevance to the field, practical implications for teaching, theoretical contributions, response to societal needs, advancement of academic knowledge, stimulation of future research, and tangible benefits for stakeholders.
keyPoints: Academic value: theoretical contribution and knowledge advancement
Pedagogical value: practical classroom and policy implications
Social value: addressing community needs and stakeholder benefits
questions.explanation: A study cannot merely claim 'this topic is important'; it must articulate how it will advance theoretical models (e.g., SLA theory), improve practical classroom instruction (pedagogical implications), and assist educational administrators, syllabus designers, and teachers (stakeholders).

questions.question: What is the distinction between the limitations and delimitations of a research study?
questions.directAnswer: Limitations are uncontrollable external constraints, while delimitations are deliberate boundaries set by the researcher.
questions.vivaAnswer: Limitations are potential weaknesses or external constraints beyond the researcher's control, such as a small sample size, short study duration, or self-report response bias. Delimitations, on the other hand, are the deliberate, intentional choices made by the researcher to narrow the scope of the study.
keyPoints: Limitations: external, uncontrollable constraints (sample access, time)
Delimitations: internal, intentional scope choices (target population, setting)
Both must be explicitly stated to establish the boundaries of claims
questions.explanation: Choosing to study only first-year undergraduate students at Jahangirnagar University is a delimitation (a researcher-chosen boundary). However, being unable to access rural colleges due to travel restrictions or students giving socially desirable questionnaire responses is a limitation.

questions.question: How do research questions, research objectives, and research hypotheses differ in function?
questions.directAnswer: A research question asks what needs answering, an objective states the concrete goal using an action verb, and a hypothesis predicts the expected empirical outcome.
questions.vivaAnswer: A research question articulates the precise inquiry guiding the study. A research objective rephrases that inquiry as an actionable operational goal using verbs like 'to determine' or 'to compare'. A research hypothesis provides a formal, testable prediction about the relationship between variables.
keyPoints: Research Question: interrogative sentence focusing the inquiry
Objective: declarative statement specifying operational aims
Hypothesis: testable prediction relating two or more variables
questions.explanation: For example: RQ: 'Does computer-assisted feedback reduce grammatical errors in L2 writing?' Objective: 'To evaluate the effect of computer-assisted feedback on grammatical error frequency.' Hypothesis: 'Students receiving computer-assisted feedback will commit significantly fewer grammatical errors than those receiving teacher-only feedback.'

questions.question: What is a research hypothesis, and how does a null hypothesis differ from an alternative hypothesis?
questions.directAnswer: A hypothesis is a testable prediction; the null hypothesis predicts no effect or difference, while the alternative hypothesis predicts a significant effect.
questions.vivaAnswer: A hypothesis is a tentative, testable proposition predicting the relationship between variables. The null hypothesis (H0) posits that there is no statistically significant difference or relationship, while the alternative hypothesis (H1) posits that an actual difference, effect, or relationship exists.
keyPoints: Hypothesis: testable, falsifiable empirical prediction
Null Hypothesis (H0): statement of no effect, no difference (baseline)
Alternative Hypothesis (H1): statement of an effect, directional or non-directional
questions.explanation: Inferential statistics specifically tests the null hypothesis. If statistical testing reveals that the probability of observing the data by chance is below the alpha threshold (p < .05), the researcher rejects the null hypothesis in favor of the alternative hypothesis.

questions.question: What is the difference between an independent variable and a dependent variable in ELT experiments?
questions.directAnswer: The independent variable is the presumed cause or intervention manipulated by the researcher, while the dependent variable is the measured outcome.
questions.vivaAnswer: The independent variable (IV) is the antecedent condition, treatment, or factor manipulated or selected by the researcher to determine its effect. The dependent variable (DV) is the consequent outcome or behaviour that is measured to determine whether the manipulation produced a change.
keyPoints: Independent Variable (IV): presumed cause, intervention, or predictor
Dependent Variable (DV): presumed effect, measured outcome
Changes in the IV are hypothesized to cause changes in the DV
questions.explanation: In a study investigating whether using subtitled English movies improves ESL listening comprehension, the instructional method (subtitled vs non-subtitled movie) is the independent variable, and the listening comprehension test score is the dependent variable.

questions.question: What is an operational definition, and why is it essential for abstract constructs like 'fluency' or 'anxiety'?
questions.directAnswer: An operational definition defines an abstract concept in terms of the concrete, observable, and measurable operations used to measure it.
questions.vivaAnswer: An operational definition translates an abstract theoretical construct into concrete, measurable procedures so it can be assessed empirically. In ELT, constructs like 'fluency' or 'anxiety' are invisible; operational definitions specify exact metrics—such as syllables spoken per second without pauses over two seconds—to ensure objective measurement and replication.
keyPoints: Converts theoretical constructs into observable, measurable indicators
Prevents subjective ambiguity in measurement
Ensures test validity, consistency, and research replicability
questions.explanation: Theoretical definitions define concepts with other abstract words (e.g., 'fluency is smooth language production'). Operational definitions specify empirical operations: 'Speaking fluency is operationalized as the mean number of words spoken per minute during a standardized three-minute picture description task.'

questions.question: What is a literature review, and what three distinct cognitive actions (summarise, synthesise, evaluate) does it demand?
questions.directAnswer: A literature review is a critical, synthesized evaluation of published research requiring scholars to summarise key points, synthesise cross-study patterns, and evaluate evidentiary quality.
questions.vivaAnswer: A literature review is a critical, structured examination of existing scholarship on a topic that establishes what is known, debated, and missing. It requires three cognitive actions: summarising the main findings of individual sources, synthesising them by connecting common themes or contradictions across studies, and evaluating the methodological strength and credibility of their evidence.
keyPoints: Summarise: stating core points accurately
Synthesise: connecting multiple sources by pattern, agreement, or disagreement
Evaluate: critically judging research credibility, limitations, and relevance
questions.explanation: A weak review merely lists studies in isolation ('Study A did X. Study B did Y'). A strong review synthesizes them comparatively ('Both Study A and Study B establish that communicative tasks increase oral fluency; however, both rely on self-report surveys, leaving actual classroom performance unmeasured').

questions.question: What are the seven types of research gaps identified in Lecture 05 of the course?
questions.directAnswer: The seven research gaps are: population/context gap, conceptual gap, empirical gap, evidence gap, theoretical gap, methodology gap, and practical gap.
questions.vivaAnswer: Lecture 05 identifies seven research gaps: population or context gap, conceptual gap, empirical gap, evidence gap, theoretical gap, methodology gap, and practical gap. Each represents an absence, contradiction, or limitation in existing scholarship that justifies a new study.
keyPoints: Population/Context: unexamined demographic or educational setting
Conceptual, Empirical, Evidence: missing definitions, data, or conflicting findings
Theoretical, Methodology, Practical: missing theory, method limits, classroom disconnect
questions.explanation: Understanding research gaps is critical for viva success. For example, an 'evidence gap' occurs when existing studies produce conflicting results. A 'methodology gap' exists when all previous studies used self-report surveys and lack observational or experimental evidence. A 'population gap' exists when a phenomenon studied in Western ESL contexts has never been investigated among rural Bangladeshi EFL learners.

questions.question: How does an annotated bibliography differ from a fully developed literature review?
questions.directAnswer: An annotated bibliography is a list of isolated source summaries with references, whereas a literature review is an integrated thematic narrative synthesizing multiple sources.
questions.vivaAnswer: An annotated bibliography provides a formal reference entry for each source followed by an individual descriptive and evaluative paragraph, treating sources separately. A literature review, in contrast, integrates multiple sources into a coherent narrative organized by themes, debates, and gaps, comparing and contrasting their findings.
keyPoints: Annotated bibliography: discrete, item-by-item reference summaries
Literature review: synthesized thematic or chronological narrative
An annotated bibliography is a preparatory reading tool, not a thesis chapter
questions.explanation: Students often make the mistake of writing literature review chapters that look like annotated bibliographies (e.g., dedicated paragraphs to single authors with no cross-study comparison). A genuine review brings multiple scholars into dialogue within each paragraph.

questions.question: What are the four common organizational structures for arranging the body of a literature review?
questions.directAnswer: The four structures are: chronological, thematic, methodological, and theoretical.
questions.vivaAnswer: The body of a literature review can be organized chronologically by historical progression of ideas, thematically by major concepts or debates, methodologically by research approaches used, or theoretically by competing explanatory theories.
keyPoints: Chronological: tracing development over time
Thematic: grouping sources by shared subtopics or core themes
Methodological: comparing quantitative, qualitative, and survey findings
Theoretical: contrasting competing theoretical frameworks
questions.explanation: Thematic organization is the most common in applied linguistics dissertations. For example, a literature review on speaking anxiety might structure sections around 'Cognitive Causes of Anxiety', 'Social Evaluation and Peer Pressure', and 'Classroom Instructional Mitigations'.

questions.question: What is a true experimental design in ELT, and why is random assignment essential?
questions.directAnswer: A true experiment manipulates an IV and measures a DV with randomized assignment of participants, which ensures initial group equivalence.
questions.vivaAnswer: A true experiment investigates cause-and-effect relationships by manipulating an independent variable, holding extraneous factors constant, and measuring changes in a dependent variable. Random assignment is essential because it probabilistically balances individual learner differences across conditions, ensuring that initial group differences do not confound the treatment effect.
keyPoints: Manipulation of independent variable (treatment)
Measurement of dependent variable (outcome)
Random assignment (R) eliminates systematic participant bias
questions.explanation: Without random assignment, an experimental group might happen to possess higher initial English proficiency, higher motivation, or better socio-economic backgrounds than the control group. Random assignment distributes these extraneous learner characteristics equally across both groups.

questions.question: How does a pretest-posttest control-group design work, and what is the formula for calculating gain score?
questions.directAnswer: Both groups are measured before and after treatment, and individual gain is calculated as posttest score minus pretest score.
questions.vivaAnswer: In a pretest-posttest control-group design, participants are randomly assigned to either an experimental or control group. Both groups take a pretest, the experimental group receives the intervention, and both take an identical or parallel posttest. The gain score is calculated as posttest minus pretest, allowing researchers to evaluate relative improvement.
keyPoints: Random assignment to experimental and control groups
Baseline measurement followed by post-intervention measurement
Gain score formula: Gain = Posttest Score - Pretest Score
questions.explanation: Experimental notation: R: O1 X O2 for the experimental group, and R: O3 - O4 for the control group. Comparing only the posttest scores is misleading if groups started with unequal initial ability. Calculating gain scores (O2 - O1 vs O4 - O3) isolates the true treatment effect.

questions.question: How does a quasi-experimental design differ from a true experiment in language classroom research?
questions.directAnswer: Quasi-experiments lack random assignment and evaluate treatments using pre-existing, intact classroom groups.
questions.vivaAnswer: A quasi-experimental design tests an instructional intervention without random assignment of individual learners, typically because institutional constraints require using pre-existing, intact classes. Because participants are not randomly assigned, researchers must statistically control for baseline differences using pretests or ANCOVA.
keyPoints: Uses intact, existing classroom groups rather than randomly assigned individuals
Common in educational settings where reassigning students disrupts schooling
Threats to internal validity (selection bias) must be addressed through pretesting
questions.explanation: In a true experiment, students are randomly assigned to Condition A or B by lottery. In a quasi-experiment, Section 1 is assigned to Condition A and Section 2 to Condition B. If Section 1 happens to have more motivated students, the outcome might be confounded by selection bias.

questions.question: What is pretest sensitization, and how does the Solomon four-group design control for it?
