questions.question: What is the difference between drawing research inferences and formulating pedagogical recommendations in a research conclusion?
questions.directAnswer: Inferences are logical conclusions drawn from the data, while recommendations are actionable, practical proposals for teachers, curriculum designers, or policymakers.
questions.vivaAnswer: Drawing research inferences involves making justified logical deductions and conceptual claims based directly on the empirical findings, answering what the evidence proves about language learning. Formulating pedagogical recommendations translates those theoretical insights into concrete, actionable advice for classroom practitioners, curriculum developers, textbook writers, and educational policymakers.
keyPoints: Inference: logical deduction grounded in data (e.g., 'Anxiety inhibits oral production')
Pedagogical recommendation: actionable classroom practice (e.g., 'Teachers should implement low-stakes pair work')
Recommendations must be realistically feasible and directly justified by the findings
questions.explanation: An inference states: 'Form-focused corrective feedback during task planning significantly improves grammatical accuracy.' The corresponding pedagogical recommendation states: 'ELT syllabus designers should integrate 5-minute pre-task grammar planning sessions into communicative writing courses.'

questions.question: What is academic plagiarism, and what are its primary forms in student research writing?
questions.directAnswer: Plagiarism is presenting someone else's work, ideas, or words as your own without proper credit; forms include direct plagiarism, patchwriting, and self-plagiarism.
questions.vivaAnswer: Plagiarism is an ethical breach involving the uncredited appropriation of another person's words, ideas, research data, or intellectual formulations, presenting them as one's own original work. Primary forms include direct plagiarism (verbatim copy-pasting without quotation marks or citation), mosaic plagiarism or patchwriting (interweaving borrowed phrases with slight word alterations without proper citation), and self-plagiarism (resubmitting one's own previously assessed academic work without authorization).
keyPoints: Unauthorized or unacknowledged use of others' text, ideas, or data
Direct plagiarism: verbatim copying without quotes and citation
Patchwriting: swapping synonyms while retaining original syntactic architecture
Self-plagiarism: re-using one's own previously submitted work without disclosure
questions.explanation: Universities enforce strict anti-plagiarism guidelines using similarity detection software like Turnitin. Jahangirnagar University syllabus for E413 explicitly stipulates that a maximum 25% similarity index is accepted for submitted dissertations.

questions.question: What is the distinction between a direct quotation, a paraphrase, and a summary in academic writing?
questions.directAnswer: A quotation reproduces exact words, a paraphrase restates an idea in original wording and syntax, and a summary condenses the broader argument of a source.
questions.vivaAnswer: A direct quotation reproduces the exact words of an author verbatim, requiring quotation marks (or a block quote for 40+ words), publication year, and specific page locator. A paraphrase restates a specific idea completely in the researcher's own original vocabulary and syntactic structure, requiring an author-year citation. A summary condenses the central thesis or extensive findings of an entire study into a brief overview in original words, also requiring citation.
keyPoints: Quotation: identical words; requires quotation marks, author, year, page (p. 12)
Paraphrase: original sentence structure and wording; requires author and year
Summary: condensed overview of an extensive work; requires author and year
questions.explanation: Changing three words in an original sentence is NOT a paraphrase; it is patchwriting. Genuine paraphrasing requires absorbing the concept and expressing it in an entirely original grammatical form.

questions.question: What is the difference between a parenthetical citation and a narrative citation in APA format?
questions.directAnswer: In a parenthetical citation, author and date appear inside parentheses; in a narrative citation, the author's name is part of the sentence with the date in parentheses.
questions.vivaAnswer: In a parenthetical citation, both the author's surname and the publication year are enclosed inside parentheses at the end of the sentence, using an ampersand for two authors (e.g., Rahman & Sen, 2024). In a narrative citation, the author's surname is embedded grammatically into the sentence structure, followed immediately by the year in parentheses, using the word 'and' for two authors (e.g., Rahman and Sen, 2024).
keyPoints: Parenthetical: (Rahman, 2024) or (Rahman & Sen, 2024) — uses '&'
Narrative: Rahman (2024) argued... or Rahman and Sen (2024) found... — uses 'and'
Both must correspond to an identical full entry in the terminal reference list
questions.explanation: Page 31 of the guide provides the clear rule: Use 'and' in narrative citations; use '&' in parenthetical citations and reference author lists.

questions.question: What is the difference between a reference list and a bibliography?
questions.directAnswer: A reference list includes only sources directly cited in the text, whereas a bibliography can include background reading consulted but not cited.
questions.vivaAnswer: In APA style, a reference list contains only the specific works that have been directly cited within the body of the paper or dissertation, establishing a one-to-one match between in-text citations and end references. A bibliography, in contrast, includes not only cited works but also background sources, foundational readings, and recommended literature that the author consulted during preparation but did not formally cite.
keyPoints: Reference list (APA): strictly 1-to-1 match with in-text citations
Bibliography: includes consulted background works not cited in text
Every cited work must be in references; every reference must be cited in text
questions.explanation: If you read an article on motivation but do not cite it anywhere in your dissertation chapters, you CANNOT include it in an APA Reference list. Doing so is an APA formatting violation.

questions.question: What are the APA 7th edition rules for using 'et al.' in in-text citations?
questions.directAnswer: For three or more authors, use 'et al.' immediately from the very first citation.
questions.vivaAnswer: Under APA 7th edition guidelines, for any work with three or more authors, the in-text citation is shortened using the first author's surname followed by 'et al.' starting from the very first citation (e.g., Rahman et al., 2024). In APA 7, 'et al.' is not italicized, and a period follows 'al' because it is an abbreviation for the Latin 'et alia' meaning 'and others'.
keyPoints: 1 author: (Rahman, 2024)
2 authors: (Rahman & Sen, 2024) parenthetically / Rahman and Sen (2024) narratively
3 or more authors: (Rahman et al., 2024) from the first citation onward
No italics on 'et al.'; period after 'al.'
questions.explanation: This represents a major update in APA 7. Under the older APA 6, works with 3 to 5 authors had to list all authors on the first citation and use 'et al.' only on subsequent citations. APA 7 streamlined this by using 'et al.' immediately from citation number one.

questions.question: How do you format a reference entry for a journal article, a whole book, and an edited book chapter in APA 7?
questions.directAnswer: Follow APA 7 templates: author surname and initials, year, sentence-case title, italics for book title or journal title/volume, and DOI.
questions.vivaAnswer: In APA 7: A book reference is formatted as: Surname, A. A. (Year). *Title of book in sentence case* (2nd ed.). Publisher. An edited book chapter is formatted as: Surname, A. A. (Year). Title of chapter. In B. B. Editor (Ed.), *Title of book* (pp. 10-25). Publisher. A journal article is formatted as: Surname, A. A., & Surname, B. B. (Year). Title of article. *Title of Journal in Title Case*, *Volume*(Issue), 45-60. https://doi.org/xxxx.
keyPoints: Book: Author. (Year). *Book title in sentence case*. Publisher.
Chapter: Author. (Year). Chapter title. In Editor (Ed.), *Book title* (pp. xx-xx). Publisher.
Journal: Author. (Year). Article title. *Journal Title in Title Case*, *Volume*(Issue), xx-xx. DOI
Journal title and volume are italicized; issue is in parentheses non-italicized
questions.explanation: Note capitalization: Book and article titles use sentence case (capitalize only first word, first word after colon, and proper nouns). Journal names keep title case and italics. In APA 7, all DOIs must be presented as active URLs beginning with https://doi.org/.

questions.question: What key updates were introduced in APA 7th edition compared to APA 6th edition regarding publisher location and DOIs?
questions.directAnswer: APA 7 omits publisher location (city/state) for books and formats DOIs as active standard URLs (https://doi.org/...).
questions.vivaAnswer: APA 7th edition introduced two major changes: first, it completely omitted the publisher's location (city and state/country) from book references, listing only the publisher name; second, it standardized Digital Object Identifiers (DOIs) as active, standardized hyperlinks starting with 'https://doi.org/', omitting the older 'doi:' prefix and 'Retrieved from' labels.
keyPoints: Publisher location (city/country) is omitted in APA 7 book citations
DOIs formatted as active standard URLs (https://doi.org/...)
Reference list author limit expanded to 20 authors before ellipsis is needed
questions.explanation: In APA 6, you wrote: 'New York, NY: Routledge.' In APA 7, you simply write: 'Routledge.' The lecture summary on Page 32 specifically clarifies this rule, noting that student templates often include outdated cities by mistake.

questions.question: What are the essential sections of a formal research proposal in applied linguistics?
questions.directAnswer: Title, Introduction and problem statement, RQs/hypotheses, Literature review, Theoretical framework, Methodology, Expected contribution, Timeline, and Budget.
questions.vivaAnswer: A comprehensive research proposal outlines a prospective study across several standard sections: a concise, informative Title; Introduction with problem statement and research significance; Research Questions, Objectives, or Hypotheses; Literature Review establishing the research gap; Theoretical or Conceptual Framework; detailed Methodology (design, sampling frame, instruments, data collection, analytical techniques, and ethical protections); Expected Scholarly Contribution; Timeline of stages; and Budget where applicable.
keyPoints: Prospective document written in future tense explaining what, why, and how
Problem statement, significance, and explicit research questions
Detailed methodology covering design, sample, instrumentation, analysis, and ethics
Timeline, budget, references, and draft research instruments in appendices
questions.explanation: A proposal demonstrates feasibility and intellectual merit. The guide emphasizes on Page 30 that a research proposal cannot report fictitious findings or results; its abstract outlines the proposed methodology and expected contributions only.

questions.question: What is the standard six-chapter structure of an ELT dissertation and the IMRAD format for academic research articles?
questions.directAnswer: Dissertations follow six core chapters: Introduction, Literature Review, Methodology, Results, Discussion, and Conclusion; research articles follow the IMRAD format.
questions.vivaAnswer: A standard ELT undergraduate or Master's dissertation consists of six core chapters: Chapter 1: Introduction; Chapter 2: Literature Review; Chapter 3: Methodology; Chapter 4: Results or Data Analysis; Chapter 5: Discussion; and Chapter 6: Conclusion and Recommendations, framed by preliminary matter (Abstract, Table of Contents) and post-matter (References, Appendices). Published empirical research articles condense this into the IMRAD structure: Introduction, Method, Results, And Discussion.
keyPoints: Six dissertation chapters: Introduction, Lit Review, Methodology, Results, Discussion, Conclusion
IMRAD journal article format: Introduction, Method, Results, And Discussion
Abstract (150-350 words) summarizes problem, method, key findings, and conclusion
questions.explanation: This six-chapter architecture represents the standard model taught across Lecture 06, 15, and the course syllabus. Preliminary pages include the 150-350 word abstract, while end matter contains APA 7 references and data collection instruments in appendices.
